info.bio: Sir James Paul McCartney (Liverpool, 18 de Junio de 1942). Cantante y compositor británico que saltó a la fama como miembro del cuarteto legendario "The Beatles". Junto a John Lennon, compañero de The Beatles, formó una de las parejas de compositores más influyentes de la música contemporánea, escribiendo conjuntamente un extenso catálogo de temas archiconocidos. Después de anunciar que dejaba el grupo (1970), McCartney empezó una exitosa carrera en solitario y formó el grupo Wings con su mujer, Linda McCartney.

scenes.name: The Beatles
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Su primer single, «Love Me Do», entró en las listas el 11 de octubre de 1962, días antes de la crisis de los misiles. En 1963 provocaron una histeria femenina sin precedentes, rompieron la deferencia de los cincuenta y, por un breve tiempo, el sistema de clases: una revolución hecha con una melodía, un flequillo y un «yeah yeah yeah». En abril de 1964 ocuparon los cinco primeros puestos de Billboard, dispararon la venta de singles y convirtieron Gran Bretaña en la «Isla Pop». Su ejemplo obligaba a componer material propio. En 1966 hay pausas súbitas dentro del impulso imparable de «Rain».

scenes.name: El underground de Londres
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En Gran Bretaña el LSD circulaba por el mismo tipo de gente que en Estados Unidos: estudiantes de arte, hipsters, bohemios y poetas, muchos llegados desde la CND. Su primera gran reunión fue la International Poetry Incarnation del Albert Hall (junio de 1965: Ginsberg, Trocchi, Burroughs, Adrian Mitchell), filmada por Peter Whitehead. En enero de 1966 John Hopkins y Steve Stollman montaron en el Marquee el primer Spontaneous Underground, intento, como los Acid Tests, de crear un entorno que se acercara a la disrupción perceptiva del LSD; el 13 de marzo, «The Trip», con el grupo de improvisación AMM y el debut en el Marquee de unos Pink Floyd que dejaban las versiones de R&B. En febrero Barry Miles y John Dunbar abrieron la librería Indica (ESP-Disk, Burroughs, Leary, Artaud, Crowley, Gurdjieff, Blavatsky), con la ayuda de Paul McCartney. En abril Miles y Hopkins repartieron en la marcha de la CND THE Global moon-edition Long Hair TIMES.

scenes.name: Alicia, la locura y el regreso a la infancia
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Al final de 1966 el LSD llevó al pop de vuelta a la infancia y a la locura. Los Beatles empezaron el 24 de noviembre «Strawberry Fields Forever», un viaje de Lennon hacia abajo, no hacia atrás, al orfanato junto a su casa, «psicoanálisis con música», unida por Geoff Emerick a partir de dos tomas; luego «When I’m Sixty-Four» y «Penny Lane». En Navidad la BBC aplazó el Alice in Wonderland de Jonathan Miller, sin cabezas de animal, con el sitar de Ravi Shankar y rodado en un hospital militar de víctimas de neurosis de guerra: un catálogo de psicosis. Grace Slick llevó «White Rabbit» a Jefferson Airplane; Syd Barrett escribía sobre el mundo de Lewis Carroll. Proliferaban los discos sobre la locura («They’re Coming to Take Me Away, Ha-Haaa!», «Pandora’s Golden Heebie Jeebies» de los Association), y en el corazón secreto del año, la tristeza frágil de «How Can We Hang On to a Dream» de Tim Hardin.

podcast.title: Birth (1942)
podcast.body: James Paul McCartney was born on June 18, 1942, to Jim and Mary McCartney. His parents met and married on April 15, 1941, under circumstances heavily influenced by World War II, including his father's exemption from military service due to a childhood ear injury and an air raid in Liverpool. "Then on June 18, 1942, they had a son. They named him James Paul McCartney."

podcast.title: Taught "Woo" Sounds by Little Richard (1962)
podcast.body: As the bass player for The Beatles, Paul McCartney was taught how to make Little Richard's distinctive "woo" vocal sounds during the two months they spent together hanging out and performing in Hamburg clubs in 1962. "teaching their bass player how he made his wool sounds when singing."

podcast.title: Groundbreaking Songwriting (1963)
podcast.body: As a member of The Beatles, Paul McCartney co-wrote (with John Lennon) over half the tracks on the band's 1963 debut album, "Please Please Me," an accomplishment described as "virtually unprecedented" for a rock and roll group of that era. "more than half of its tracks were written by John Lennon and Paul McCartney, a virtually unprecedented achievement for a rock and roll group."

podcast.title: "Washed Up" Criticism (1973)
podcast.body: In 1973, critics declared Paul McCartney "all washed up," arguing that competing with his past self from The Beatles was his greatest challenge. His new band, Wings, was often criticized for producing "nothing more than silly love songs" as they prepared to record his fifth album, *Band on the Run*. "In 1973 is the same year that critics said that Paul McCartney was all washed up because there may have been nothing more difficult for Paul McCartney than competing with Paul McCartney."

podcast.title: Acquisition of Norvat Jack Music (1973)
podcast.body: Following the loss of The Beatles' publishing, McCartney began acquiring other artists' catalogs in 1973, starting with Norvat Jack Music, which held many songs by his idol, Buddy Holly. This established a significant income stream for him. "He started in 1973 buying a company called Norvat Jack Music, which contained many of the songs by Buddy Holly, one of McCartney's idols."

podcast.body: McCartney was outbid by Michael Jackson for the ATV Music catalog in 1985, a catalog that included The Beatles' songs, for which Jackson paid $47.5 million. McCartney was "not pleased" by this turn of events. "Jackson then outbid McCartney, paying $47.5 million for this catalog. Maca was not pleased."

podcast.title: Early RealVideo Stream (1999)
podcast.body: A Paul McCartney concert from Liverpool in 1999 was broadcast via RealVideo, serving as an early experiment in streaming audio and video. The quality was described as poor ("an image a little bigger than a post-it stamp with glitchy video and terrible sound"), but it demonstrated the technology's potential. "I remember watching a real video broadcast of a Paul McCartney show from Liverpool in 1999."

podcast.title: Celery Contribution to Super Furry Animals Album (2001)
podcast.body: Paul McCartney provided a unique audio contribution to the Welsh band Super Furry Animals' 2001 album "Rings Around the World." When asked to appear on their record, he sent a tape solely containing a recording of himself munching on celery, which the band subsequently used in their song "Receptacle for the Respectable." "When they arrived, it was a recording of Paul munching on some celery."

podcast.title: Income from Rights Management (2016)
podcast.body: Paul McCartney, earning around 60 million dollars and ranking between positions 26 and 27, continues to generate significant income despite not releasing much new material. His earnings are largely due to the intelligent management of his own solo career rights and, more significantly, the rights to The Beatles' discography. He has actively repurchased a substantial portion of these rights from Michael Jackson's estate, who previously owned virtually all of them, in an effort to recover income he had not received for nearly 40 years. "está ganando es mucho dinero, gracias a una gestión muy inteligente de los derechos de los Beatles y de su carrera solitario."

podcast.body: After 50 years, Paul McCartney finally regained control of his music in 2017, following a successful lawsuit related to a new American copyright law. "And in 2017, a court ruled in his favor. So after 50 years, Paul McCartney finally regains control of his music."

podcast.title: "Paul is Dead" Theory
podcast.body: A multi-layered story claimed that Paul McCartney died in a car accident in November 1966 and was subsequently replaced by a Canadian lookalike. This imposter allegedly featured in everything from the *Sgt. Pepper* album artwork onwards. "Paul McCartney was the subject of a weird, multi-layered story that had him die in a car accident in November 1966 and then replaced by a Canadian lookalike."

podcast.title: Accidental Feedback Discovery
podcast.body: On October 18, 1964, during a recording session at Abbey Road Studios, Paul McCartney accidentally initiated the controlled feedback sound that would be used on "I Feel Fine." He plucked a string on his bass, and when John Lennon laid his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp, the guitar picked up the bass note and started feeding back. Paul and John recognized the coolness of the sound and requested producer George Martin to record it. "The discovery began when Paul McCarty picked a string on his bass, Appropole of Nothing, and then John laid his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp and started to walk away."

podcast.body: Paul McCartney had three children with Linda McCartney: Stella, a fashion designer; Mary, a vegetarian activist and photographer; and James, the only musician among them, who has appeared on albums by both Paul and Linda and has his own records. xref.title: Birth (1942)
xref.body: James Paul McCartney was born on June 18, 1942, to Jim and Mary McCartney. His parents met and married on April 15, 1941, under circumstances heavily influenced by World War II, including his father's exemption from military service due to a childhood ear injury and an air raid in Liverpool. "Then on June 18, 1942, they had a son. They named him James Paul McCartney."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Paul McCartney's Birth (1942)
xref.body: Paul McCartney was born on June 18, 1942, to Jim and Mary McCartney, whose meeting and marriage on April 15, 1941, was an indirect consequence of World War II. Jim McCartney's exemption from military service due to a childhood ear injury (from falling off a wall in 1912) and the timing of a German Luftwaffe bombing raid in Liverpool in 1941, which led him to his mother's place where Mary was visiting, are cited as critical events leading to their union and Paul's birth. "Then on June 18, 1942, they had a son. They named him James Paul McCartney."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: 1958 Percy Phillips Home Recording – "That'll Be the Day" / "In Spite of All the Danger"
xref.body: An ultra-rare, two-sided 78 RPM disc from 1958, recorded by John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, pianist John Lowe, and drummer Colin Hanton at the home of Percy Phillips, who specialized in "down and dirty" recordings in his front room. Side one features Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day," and side two contains "In Spite of All the Danger," the first-ever Lennon-McCartney recording. This record is owned by Paul McCartney and is estimated to be worth at least 100,000 pounds if it were ever to be sold. "The result was a two-sided 78 RPM disc with Buddy Holly's That'll Be the Day on Side One, and the first ever Lennon McCartney recording on the other, in spite of all the danger."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initial Publishing Control by Northern Songs (February 1963)
xref.body: In February 1963, The Beatles' music publishing was managed by Northern Songs, a company owned by Dick James, their manager Brian Epstein, John Lennon, and Paul McCartney. "In the beginning, this would be February 1963, the publishing for the Beatles music was handled by a company called Northern Songs. The owners were Dick James, Manager Brian Epstein, John Lennon, and Paul McCarty."

xref.title: King Edward Hotel Frenzy (1964)
xref.body: Upon their arrival at the King Edward Hotel in downtown Toronto on September 6, 1964, a frenzy of fans greeted The Beatles, leading to Paul McCartney having his shirt torn and Ringo Starr being separated from John and George. Although police quickly restored order on the street, Beatlemania continued inside, where a 14-year-old girl was found hiding in the linen closet of their royal suite. "Paul would have a shirt torn open by a fan, wrangle with separated from John and George, but thankfully police were able to quickly restore order on the street and get the band into the hotel."

xref.title: Paul McCartney Greets Winnipeg (1964)
xref.body: Following the incident with Bryce Decker at the Winnipeg airport on August 18, 1964, Paul McCartney exited the plane, yelled "Hello, Winnipeg," and descended the stairs, where he was immediately swarmed by a throng of reporters, including Bob Burns. This brief appearance was the band's only direct interaction with the Winnipeg crowd, as they never returned to the city. "Oh, and the man who greeted the crowd was none other than Paul McCartney."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dick James Sells Share to ATV Music (Post-1967)
xref.body: After Brian Epstein's death in 1967, The Beatles' business affairs became chaotic. Relations with Dick James soured, leading him to sell his share of Northern Songs to ATV Music without informing John Lennon and Paul McCartney, who were upset and attempted unsuccessfully to buy James's share themselves. "After Manager Brian Epstein died in 1967, the business affairs of the Beatles were in shambles. Relations between the group and Dick James music soured, and Dick James wanted out of Northern Songs. That's when he sold his share to a company called ATV Music without giving any notice to John and Paul."

xref.title: Percussionist for "Live and Let Die" (1973)
xref.body: Ray Cooper, a renowned percussionist who has collaborated with a wide range of artists including Elton John, Pink Floyd, and Eric Clapton, played percussion on Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. His involvement brought a significant rhythmic element to the globally successful rock song. "The percussionist on that song is Ray Cooper who has worked with everyone from Elton John to Pink Floyd to Eric Clapton."

xref.title: Post-Beatles Collaboration with McCartney (1973)
xref.body: George Martin, who built and ran Air Studios in London, agreed to produce the recording sessions for Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. This marked a significant reunion, as it was the first time Martin had worked with a Beatle since the conclusion of the "Abbey Road" sessions in 1969. Martin later compelled the Bond producers to use McCartney's version as the title sequence. "Martin agreed to produce the sessions marking this as the first time since the end of the Abbey Road sessions that he got to work with a beetle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer's Ultimatum for "Live and Let Die" (1973)
xref.body: George Martin delivered an ultimatum to the Bond film producers regarding Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. He informed them that if they wanted the "very good theme song," they would have to use Paul's version for the title sequence, otherwise they would need to find someone else for their movie. Faced with time constraints, the producers, either Harry Saltzman or Albert Broccoli, conceded. "When it was done George Martin went to the producers and said look we've got a very good theme song for you but the only way you're going to get it is if you use Paul's version as the title sequence."

xref.title: Songs Acquired by Paul McCartney (1973)

xref.title: Glenn Matlock's Departure (February 1977)
xref.body: Matlock's departure was officially reported as a firing in February 1977 because he "liked The Beatles too much," specifically Paul McCartney, and allegedly washed his feet too often. This narrative was fabricated and fed to the press by manager Malcolm McLaren. In truth, Matlock quit due to intense friction with Johnny Rotten, McLaren's manipulative "head games," constant media attacks, canceled gigs, venue bans, lack of pay, and the physical assaults suffered by Johnny and Paul. "Glenn Matlock was fired in February 1977... Matlock wasn't fired. He quit."

xref.title: 1981 Reissue of "That'll Be the Day"
xref.body: In 1981, Paul McCartney reissued The Quarrymen's recording of "That'll Be the Day." These reissues were made in limited runs of 25 copies for both 10-inch 78s and 7-inch 45s, and are now highly valuable, fetching close to $20,000 each. "McCartney reassured that recording in 1981 on both 10-inch 78s and 7-inch 45s in lots of 25 each."

xref.title: Received Publishing Advice from Paul McCartney (1983)
xref.body: In 1983, Paul McCartney advised Michael Jackson on the lucrative nature of publishing, famously telling him, "He who owns the publishing controls the world." This advice significantly influenced Jackson. "The money is in publishing, Mac and console Jacko. He who owns the publishing controls the world. And this was advice that Jackson never forgot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Acquisition of ATV Music (1985)
xref.body: In 1985, Michael Jackson outbid Paul McCartney to purchase the ATV Music catalog for $47.5 million. This catalog included 4,000 songs, notably 250 by The Beatles (almost their entire output), as well as tracks by The Rolling Stones, Elvis, and Bruce Springsteen. "In 1985, ATV Music, that company with the Beatles publishing, went up for sale. Four thousand songs, including 250 from the Beatles, which is pretty much everything they ever wrote, as well as tracks by the Rolling Stones, Elvis and Bruce Springsteen. Jackson then outbid McCartney, paying $47.5 million for this catalog."

xref.title: Acquisition of Beatles Publishing Catalog (1985)
xref.body: On August 15, 1985, Michael Jackson purchased a substantial portion of The Beatles' publishing catalog, granting him significant control over their music. This ownership allowed him to authorize the licensing of "Revolution" for the controversial 1987 Nike commercial, despite the objections of the surviving Beatles. "Because on August 15, 1985, he'd bought a huge chunk of the Beatles publishing catalog right out from underneath Paul McCartney's nose."

xref.title: "Her Majesty" - Accidental Hidden Track
xref.body: The inclusion of "Her Majesty" as a hidden track on "Abbey Road" was an unintended consequence of studio procedure. After Paul McCartney requested the song's removal, tape assistant John Kerlander snipped it out and spliced it to the end of the master tape with 20 seconds of blank tape, in accordance with Abbey Road's rules for edited material. A mastering engineer either overlooked or misread Kerlander's note, resulting in the song's presence on the final master, which the Beatles found "really cool" and decided to keep. "And so the first hidden track came to be as the result of an accident."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Now and Then" - AI-Assisted Song (2020s)
xref.body: The Beatles created a brand new song, "Now and Then," utilizing artificial intelligence technology. Film director Peter Jackson was able to isolate John Lennon's vocals from a "bad sounding 1978 cassette demo," allowing Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr to add new parts, alongside George Harrison's contributions from a 1995 session. "But then we can point to what the Beatles did with AI and the song Now and Then, using brand new technology. Film director Peter Jackson was able to isolate John's vocals from a bad sounding 1978 cassette demo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Abbey Road Studios' Editing Policy
xref.body: A specific rule at Abbey Road Studios mandated that any material edited out from a master tape had to be retained at the end of the tape for future reference. This policy, followed by tape assistant John Kerlander when Paul McCartney requested "Her Majesty" be removed from "Abbey Road", inadvertently led to the creation of the album's hidden track. "The rules at Abby Road said that any material edited out from a master tape had to be left at the end of the tape for reference."

xref.title: Accidental Feedback Discovery
xref.body: On October 18, 1964, while at Abbey Road Studios, John Lennon accidentally discovered the controlled feedback sound used on "I Feel Fine." After Paul McCartney plucked a bass string, John leaned his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp and began to walk away, inadvertently causing the guitar to pick up the bass note and create feedback. Recognizing the unique sound, both Lennon and McCartney asked producer George Martin to capture it for their new song. "But then the guitar picked up the sound of that bass note and started feeding back, and the sound was really cool, but a total accident."

xref.title: Band Name Origin
xref.body: Douglas Colvin, a huge Paul McCartney fan, knew McCartney sometimes used the alias "Paul Ramon" (after producer Phil Ramon) on hotel registers. Douglas adopted "D.D. Ramon." The plural, "Ramones," sounded like a gang, and as no other names clicked, it stuck. To reinforce a "gang mentality," all members adopted "Ramone" as their surname, deciding to appear as brothers, and wore leather jackets, jeans, and t-shirts. "Douglas liked the sound of that, so he started calling himself D.D. Ramon... The plural of Ramon, Ramon's, sounded like it could be the name of a gang."

"Veronica was co-written by Costello with former Beatle Paul McCartney."

xref.title: Collaborations and Friendship
xref.body: James McCartney has appeared on albums by both his father, Paul McCartney, and his mother, Linda McCartney. He became friends with other Beatles offspring—Danny Harrison, Zach Starkey, and Sean Lennon—and they entertained the idea of forming a band, though it didn't come to fruition. "He's appeared on albums by both Paul and Linda and has several records of his own. He eventually became friends with Danny Harrison, son of George, Zach Starky, son of Ringo, and Sean Lennon, son of John. They floored with the idea of forming their own band. Imagine that, but nothing ever came of it."

xref.title: Developing Mop Top Haircut (Astrid Kircher)
xref.body: About a year after the initial cut by Yurgen Volmer, during The Beatles' extended residency in Hamburg, Astrid Kircher regularly cut their hair into this new look. She first applied the cut to Stu Sutcliffe, then George Harrison, and finally John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Within two years, as The Beatles became the biggest band globally, their haircuts were nearly as famous as their music, solidifying long hair on men as a lasting trend. "She first gave the cut to Stu, and then George, and then finally John and Paul."

xref.title: EMI Audition Demo (Undated) – "Hello Little Girl" / "Till There Was You" Acetate
xref.body: A one-of-a-kind, 10-inch acetate test pressing recorded as an audition for EMI Records, representing the first record featuring the Beatles as they would become known. Side A features "Hello Little Girl," credited to Paul McCartney and the Beatles, while Side B has "Till There Was You," credited to John Lennon and the Beatles; manager Brian Epstein wrote the titles in blue pen to ensure fairness. This record disappeared for decades before being found in the attic of Les Maguire, a member of Gerry and the Pacemakers. It was sold in March 2016 for 77,500 pounds, equivalent to $95,000 American or $130,000 Canadian. "It's a 10-inch acetate, a test pressing in other words, and is a one-of-a-kind thing Hello Little Girl on the A side, and Till There Was You on the B side."

xref.title: Management Crisis and Disagreement (Post-Epstein)
xref.body: After the death of their manager Brian Epstein, The Beatles faced a management crisis. Three members of the band favored appointing Rolling Stones manager Alan Klein to handle their affairs. However, Paul McCartney wished to work with his father-in-law, Lee Eastman, an entertainment lawyer who managed the finances of many musicians. This fundamental disagreement over management created significant tension within the group. "And that tension, that disagreement went a long way towards ending the Beatles."

xref.title: Musical Development and Hard Rock Focus
xref.body: By 1967, Nancy and Ann were performing as The Viewpoints, with Nancy also doing solo shows influenced by Joni Mitchell and Paul Simon, as well as rock figures like John Lennon, Paul McCartney, Jimi Hendrix, and Jimmy Page. As their groups evolved into Heart, Nancy increasingly focused on hard rock and discovered drop D tuning, a technique that would become vital to the grunge era 15 years later. "By the time some of the various groups she was in with Ann evolved into Hart, Nancy had become much more focused on hard rock and she discovered drop D tuning, something that would become essential to the grunge era 15 years later."

xref.title: Name Origin (Paul McCartney Connection)

Dee Dee, already calling himself Dee Dee Ramone, suggested "The Ramones" for the band to signify unity and family. "DD was a big fan of Paul McCartney and the Beatles, and the days of the Silver Beatles, Paul McCartney used to check on two hotel rooms using the alias Paul Ramone."

xref.title: Origin of Mop Top Haircut (Yurgen Volmer)
xref.body: In 1961, Paul McCartney and John Lennon met Yurgen Volmer in Paris, who was a friend of Astrid Kircher and Stu Sutcliffe. Volmer had long hair parted and worn over his forehead, which "entranced" Lennon and McCartney, who still wore their hair slicked back. They asked him to cut their hair in his style, giving birth to the first version of the Beatles' mop top. "So he cut their hair, and so the Beatles' mop top was born, or at least the first version of it."

xref.title: Origin of Sergeant Pepper Mustaches
xref.body: In late 1966, all members of The Beatles began growing mustaches, a fashion choice prominently featured on the artwork for their "Sergeant Pepper" album the following year. This trend originated after Paul McCartney had a moped crash, resulting in a face injury and a scar on his lip from bad stitches. He grew a mustache to conceal the scar, and the rest of the band followed suit. "Paul McCarty had a crash on a moat pad, which resulted in a faceplant on the pavement and this left a scar on his lip due to some bad stitches. And he became self-conscious of the scar. He grew a mustache and the rest of the band followed."

"Douglas liked the sound of that, so he started calling himself D.D. Ramon... The plural of Ramon, Ramon's, sounded like it could be the name of a gang."

xref.title: Paul McCartney and Linda Eastman - Family Ties
xref.body: Paul McCartney married Linda Eastman, leading to his introduction to her father, Lee Eastman. Lee was an entertainment lawyer who was known for handling the finances of numerous musicians. "When Paul McCartney married Linda Eastman, Macco was introduced to her father Lee, who was an entertainment lawyer, who handled the finances of a lot of musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Paul McCartney's "Paul Ramone" Alias
xref.body: Dee Dee Ramone, a big fan of Paul McCartney, adopted the "Ramone" surname because McCartney used to check into hotel rooms under the alias "Paul Ramone" during the days of The Silver Beatles. "DD was a big fan of Paul McCartney and the Beatles, and the days of the Silver Beatles, Paul McCartney used to check on two hotel rooms using the alias Paul Ramone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Paul McCartney's Original Copy of "That'll Be the Day"
xref.body: Paul McCartney possesses the singular original recording of Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day" by his pre-Beatles band, The Quarrymen, with its estimated value being around $250,000 US. "Paul McCartney owns the one and only original copy, and its estimated value is in the vicinity of 250,000 US."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Paul McCartney's Shock and Subsequent Catalog Acquisitions
xref.body: Paul McCartney was "especially stunned" by the loss of his Beatles' publishing rights. This experience motivated him to invest heavily in music catalogs, beginning in 1973 with the purchase of Norvat Jack Music, which included songs by his idol Buddy Holly, establishing a significant income stream from controlled catalogs. "Paul McCartney was especially stunned by this. He learned the hard way about the value of owning the publishing-depository music. So if he couldn't own his own music, the music he made with the Beatles, he decided that he would bulk up his financial holdings by buying the catalogs of others. He started in 1973 buying a company called Norvat Jack Music, which contained many of the songs by Buddy Holly"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Breakup Media Feud
xref.body: After The Beatles broke up, Paul McCartney and John Lennon frequently engaged in public disputes through the media. "But after the Beatles broke up, Paul and John scrapped a lot in the media."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Smiths Career as Session Guitarist
xref.body: After The Smiths' breakup, Johnny Marr became a highly sought-after session guitarist. He worked and toured with The Pretenders and Dada, and later co-founded Electronic with Barney Sumner of New Order. He also became a friend and confidante of Noel Gallagher of Oasis, collaborating with him in the studio, and worked with artists like Beth Orton, Neil Finn, Paul McCartney, and Talking Heads. "Meanwhile, Johnny Mar became a very hot session guitarist, working in touring with the pretenders in Dada."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Potential Future Buyers
xref.body: Paul McCartney and Andrew Lloyd Webber have publicly stated their willingness to purchase Abbey Road Studios if it were ever put up for sale again. "And if it were to be put up for sale, people like Paul McCartney and Andrew Lloyd Webber have said that they'd be up for buying it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Songs Remain with Sony Until After 2050
xref.body: Despite Paul McCartney regaining control of his music, John Lennon's songs will remain with Sony until 70 years after his death, meaning his heirs will not benefit from the income until sometime after 2050. "John Lennon's songs, however, will remain with Sony until 70 years after his death. None of his errors will see the benefit of that money until sometime after 2050."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unhappy with Dick James' Sale of Northern Songs
xref.body: John Lennon was not happy when Dick James sold his share of Northern Songs to ATV Music without prior notice to him and Paul McCartney, and they unsuccessfully tried to buy James's share themselves. "That's when he sold his share to a company called ATV Music without giving any notice to John and Paul. They were not happy about this and offered to buy Dick James share."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unofficial Mascot of Corinthians Soccer Team
xref.body: Taylor Swift serves as the unofficial mascot for the Brazilian soccer team Corinthians, based in Sao Paulo, due to a phenomenon known as the "Taylor Swift rule." Since 2006, the team has never lost a game whenever she releases an album. Conversely, the team consistently loses immediately after Paul McCartney releases a new record. "Going back to 2006, the team has never lost a game when Tate releases an album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: World-Renowned Percussionist and Collaborator
xref.body: Jody Linscott is recognized as probably "the world's most famous female percussionist" due to her extensive work with numerous major artists. She has toured with Paul McCartney, Jay-Z, Phil Collins, Santana, The Who, and Sheila E., and her percussion can be heard on many of Prince's biggest records, demonstrating a long and celebrated career. "She is probably the world's most famous female percussionist. She is all over Prince's biggest records and has a long discography and performance resume of her own."
